title: is_pause_process() reads only the first 4096 bytes of /proc/<pid>/environ, so a live pause process is treated as stale
body:
Since #28323, when podman fails to join the namespaces named by `pause.pid`, it
decides whether that PID is really a pause process by looking for
`_PODMAN_PAUSE=1` in `/proc/<pid>/environ`, and deletes `pause.pid` when it
doesn't find it. That lookup reads a single 4096-byte chunk. But
`_PODMAN_PAUSE` is added with `setenv()` just before the pause process is
forked (`rootless_linux.c:1102`), so it sits at the *end* of the environment
block — which means any session with more than 4 KB of environment fails the
check, and a perfectly healthy pause process has its pid file removed.

The comment above the read says the entry is searched for in chunks, but there
is only one `read()` (`pkg/rootless/rootless_linux.c:645`, main at `fb1cb4fa6ea4`):

```c
  const size_t buf_size = 4096;
  ...
  /* Read in chunks and search for the null-delimited key=value entry.  */
  n = TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY (read (fd, buf, buf_size));
  if (n <= 0)
    return 0;
```

The Go twin of the same predicate doesn't have this problem —
`isPauseProcess()` in `rootless_linux.go` uses `os.ReadFile` and reads the
whole thing. Only the C constructor path is affected.

### Reproducing it

The function is self-contained, so this needs neither podman nor root. Copy
`is_pause_process()` verbatim out of `rootless_linux.c` into a file, add
`#include <errno.h>` for `TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY`, drop the `cleanup_*` attributes,
and add a `main()` that takes a PID in `argv[1]` and prints three things: the
size of that process's environ, whether it contains `_PODMAN_PAUSE=1`, and what
`is_pause_process()` answers. Then start two processes that differ only in how
much padding they carry:

```console
$ env -i PAD=short _PODMAN_PAUSE=1 sleep 120 & SMALL=$!
$ env -i PAD=$(printf 'x%.0s' $(seq 1 4200)) _PODMAN_PAUSE=1 sleep 120 & BIG=$!
```

```console
$ ./pause-check $SMALL
environ = 26 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(1363760) = 1

$ ./pause-check $BIG
environ = 4221 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(1363761) = 0
```

Both carry the entry; only the size of the environment differs. It is
deterministic and single-threaded — no race involved.

Against the real pause processes on this machine, same result:

```console
$ ./pause-check 1176175
environ = 4515 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(1176175) = 0

$ ./pause-check 2693103
environ = 4377 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(2693103) = 0
```

Those two were created by podman 5.8.4, which predates #28323 and so never runs
the check — but `setenv ("_PODMAN_PAUSE", "1", 1)` is byte-identical there
(`v5.8.4:770` and `main:1102`), so the environment layout a 6.x pause process
gets is the same one shown above.

### What I haven't verified

I have not watched podman 6 actually delete a valid `pause.pid`. This machine
runs 5.8.4, which doesn't carry the code, and I didn't want to reproduce the
consequence on a live system. What is demonstrated above is that the predicate
returns the wrong answer for genuine pause processes; the `unlink()` follows
from it directly at the three call sites in the constructor
(`rootless_linux.c:891`, `:897`, `:903`).

### How much this matters

Less than it first looks, and worth being precise about: the check only runs
*after* `open_namespace()` or `setns()` has already failed, so it never fires on
a healthy path. What it changes is the outcome of a failure that would otherwise
be transient. Instead of that one command failing, `pause.pid` is deleted, and
the next podman command builds a second pause process — a sibling user
namespace, not an ancestor. Containers still running in the first one become
unmanageable: `podman ps` goes on reporting them `Up`, while `exec`, `stop` and
`kill` fail with messages that point at the wrong layer entirely
(`unable to find user root: no matching entries in passwd file`,
`crun: kill: Operation not permitted`, `Error: operation not permitted`).

I have been in exactly that state, though not through this bug — it happened on
5.8.4 for a reason I never managed to establish, so I'm not claiming a causal
link, and that is not what I'm reporting here. I mention it only because of how
long it took to understand: four containers running for a day and a half, all
listed as `Up`, none of them reachable, and nothing anywhere suggesting
`podman system migrate`, which is the way out.

It will also look intermittent, because whether it bites depends on the
environment size of whichever process first brought the pause process up. On
this desktop the numbers sit right on the boundary — plasmashell 2809 B, an
interactive shell 3946 B, the two pause processes 4515 B and 4377 B.

### Suggested direction

The small fix is to read the whole file rather than one chunk, which also makes
the C side agree with the Go side that already does this.

The alternative is to stop asking `environ` in the first place — the question
being answered is "is this the process I think it is", and a check that doesn't
depend on how big someone's environment happens to be would be sturdier. That's
a design call rather than a bug fix, so I've only mentioned it.

### Related hardening, not the defect above

Whatever the buffer ends up being, the scan can walk past what was actually
read. `read()` may stop mid-entry, leaving the tail of `buf` with no NUL in it;
`strcmp (p, ...)` and `strlen (p)` then run past `buf + n`, and when
`n == buf_size` past the end of the allocation. Bounding the scan by `n` seems
worth doing regardless of how the size question is settled.

### Environment

- podman 5.8.4 (`podman-5.8.4-1.fc44.x86_64`, Fedora RPM), rootless, cgroups v2,
  crun 1.28, catatonit 0.2.1
- Fedora 44, kernel 7.1.9-200.fc44.x86_64, KDE Plasma Wayland session
- Code read and quoted from `main` at `fb1cb4fa6ea4`; also present in `v6.1.0`,
  absent from `v5.8.4` and `v5.8.6`

comments.body: Could we just use `clearenv()` before `setenv()` to not have to deal with that?
